summary: Furrow is a crop rotation planner. It simulates a farmer’s current crop rotation—as well as potential alternatives—using 22 years of historical weather data from NASA for the specific field in question. It then compares these options based on profitability, soil erosion, carbon levels, and water usage, including projections for a warmer and drier climate. A machine learning model, utilizing NASA HLS imagery and USDA crop maps, identifies exactly what is being grown on each plot and when the land lies bare. Ultimately, this allows farmers to make data-driven decisions about their crop rotations, rather than relying on guesswork.
details:
Furrow helps farmers see how their land is changing and which crop rotation will still pay off in a hotter, drier climate. It combines three layers for every field: how the climate has shifted, what the soil allows, and how the land is actually being used.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Climate: daily NASA POWER weather for 2002–2023 is used to replay each season. We then run a stress scenario (+2 °C, −10% rain) to test which rotations survive. For East Kazakhstan, the current rotation drops from a small profit to a loss per hectare, while the best alternative stays profitable.

2. Soil water: a simple water-balance model is checked against NASA SMAP root-zone soil moisture on 340 dates (r = 0.60); GPM IMERG rainfall gives the same ranking.

3. Land use (machine learning): from NASA HLS satellite scenes (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, 30 m, 22 cloud-free dates in 2021) we compute NDVI and SWIR time series for every pixel. A RandomForest classifier, trained on USDA Cropland Data Layer labels, identifies the crop on each field, the months when soil was left bare, and the 2019–2021 crop history.

VALIDATION

We used spatial block cross-validation with buffers, so the model is always tested on areas it never saw. Accuracy on farm pixels: 0.89 (RandomForest + field history), compared with 0.46 for always guessing the most common crop. A model trained on 2021 keeps the same crop accuracy (0.86) on 2020. We also fine-tuned the NASA/IBM foundation model Prithvi-EO-2.0 on the same images: 0.84, on par with RandomForest, so we kept the lighter model for the product. Known limits: fallow land is still confused with desert, small grains are rare in the training area, and the ML part is validated on one 17 × 17 km area in Arizona.

OUTPUT

The web app shows, for each plot, the crop, its 2019–2021 history, bare-soil months and a confidence note, next to the climate and soil layers. The ML module exports 752 plots of about 0.7 km² for the map.

IMPACT

Instead of regional averages, a farmer sees their own field: how the climate moved, what the soil allows, how the land is used today, and which rotation still makes money. Everything runs on open NASA data, so the approach can move to regions without official crop maps, such as East Kazakhstan, given a small set of local labels.

TOOLS

Python (scikit-learn, rasterio, NumPy, pandas, earthaccess), PyTorch for Prithvi fine-tuning on a GTX 1050 Ti, React + TypeScript + Leaflet for the web app, H3 grid for map cells.

USE OF AI TOOLS

AI assistants (Claude) were used to help write and review code, documentation and presentation text. All data processing, model training and validation results were produced by running our own code on the listed datasets. Prithvi-EO-2.0 is a foundation model used as a comparison experiment.
